claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a closely matched high-entropy-alloy derivative has high saturation magnetization.
The baseline alloy typically has coercivity no greater than 100 Oe.
The proposed intervention is addition of 0.5–1 wt.% carbon during alloy processing.
Adding 0.5–1 wt.% carbon to fcc FeCoNi will induce in situ carbide precipitation.
The resulting carbides will be nanoscale, finely dispersed, and embedded in the fcc matrix.
The carbide nanoprecipitates will act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning by the nanoprecipitates will hinder magnetic-domain-wall movement.
Hindered domain-wall movement will increase coercivity.
Carbon addition will increase coercivity by at least 20–30% relative to an undoped matched baseline.
For a baseline coercivity of approximately 100 Oe, the carbon-modified alloy will reach at least approximately 120–130 Oe.
The coercivity increase will occur without significantly reducing saturation magnetization.
The overall fcc matrix can be preserved after addition of 0.5–1 wt.% carbon.
The carbon-modified material must retain a single-phase fcc structure.
Coercivity and saturation magnetization will be assessed at room temperature by conventional hysteresis magnetometry, specifically VSM.
XRD and TEM can be used to verify retention of the fcc matrix and TEM can confirm the presence and dispersion of carbide nanoprecipitates.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires carbide nanoprecipitates, which constitute a second phase, while also requiring the modified material to remain single-phase fcc. Retaining an fcc matrix is compatible with carbides, but retaining an entirely single-phase fcc structure is not.

The baseline is allowed to be any value at or below 100 Oe, but the numerical prediction and falsification language are anchored to approximately 100 Oe. For a substantially lower matched baseline, a successful 20–30% relative increase could still remain well below 100 Oe, making 'remains at or near 100 Oe' an inconsistent falsification condition.
